NASA is investing in additive manufacturing across multiple mission directorates, including Aeronautics, Science, Human Exploration, and Space Technology.
At Langley Research Center, additive manufacturing is enabling the design of lightweight, high-performance aircraft structures with tailored materials and geometries.
Glenn Research Center is working to develop fully non-metallic gas turbine engines using additive manufacturing of polymer and ceramic matrix composites.
NASA has successfully tested additively manufactured rocket engine injectors and thrust chamber assemblies, achieving significant reductions in part count, welds, and machining operations.
Additive manufacturing techniques can create complex internal geometries for environmental control and life support systems, as well as tools, on the International Space Station.
Goddard Space Flight Center has flown the first additively manufactured component in space, a battery case on a suborbital sounding rocket mission.

The National Research Council report identified key challenges in transitioning additive manufacturing to space environments, including the need to resolve fundamental technical issues and the requirement for supporting infrastructure.

NASA's vision for in-space manufacturing includes a progression from initial 3D printing demonstrations on the ISS to the ability to print entire spacecraft and utilize in-situ resources on the Moon, Mars, and other destinations.

NASA is investing in cross-cutting research to understand the relationships between additive manufacturing processing, material structure, and part properties, with the goal of developing standardized qualification methodologies.
NASA is working to develop foundational non-destructive evaluation (NDE) methodologies for certifying additive manufactured parts and materials, particularly for critical aerospace components.
NASA is collaborating with industry, other government agencies, universities, and research institutions to advance additive manufacturing capabilities and address key challenges.

NASA centers are exploring a variety of additive manufacturing techniques, including selective laser melting, electron beam freeform fabrication, binder jetting, fused deposition modeling, and aerosol jet printing.
The International Space Station is being used as a testbed to demonstrate key in-space manufacturing technologies, such as the first 3D printer in space and the printing of electronic components.

NASA's in-space manufacturing technology development vision includes milestones for ground-based demonstrations, ISS utilization, and the eventual capability to produce a wide range of items, including entire spacecraft, on the Moon, Mars, and other destinations.

Additive manufacturing is seen as a key enabler for transforming space architectures and enabling new capabilities that were previously not possible or too difficult to manufacture and launch from Earth.
